title: Incremental assertive toolflow and SDK thermostat — PRD (WIP)
body:
Summary
This is a working PRD for a new hosted-api pattern were calling the \"assertive toolflow\" with an SDK-facing \"thermostat\" concept. The goal: let client SDKs and the server coordinate incremental, typed outputs and opportunistic tool invocations while trading off latency vs fidelity automatically. This doc covers protocol primitives, SDK ergonomics, basic rollout plan, and acceptance criteria.

Problem / motivation
- Teams building multi-tool experiences need deterministic result shapes (structured output) but also care deeply about tail latency and cost.
- Current approach (full blocking tool chains or ad-hoc speculative calls) forces either high latency at 1x fidelity or brittle client-side heuristics.
- We want a single runtime-friendly pattern to support: quick partial replies, optional later enrichments via tool calls, and clear developer expectations for eventual committed outputs.

Key idea (short)
- Server and SDK negotiate a lightweight, incremental contract for a request: the SDK provides a fidelity budget (thermostat) and hints; the server produces an initial assertive partial response (structured frame) and then optionally runs toollets to enrich the response, issuing update frames with merge/commit semantics. The SDK exposes simple knobs so product engineers can pick latency-first or fidelity-first defaults per route.

Objectives (measurable)
- 95th percentile first-byte latency for common microturns <= current baseline (no tool calls) + 15% within first rollout.
- Reduce per-request cost for low-fidelity queries by >= 30% via early partial replies and conditional tool execution on 50% of applicable requests.
- SDK ergonomics: 80% of internal teams can switch to thermostat defaults without changing server code in pilot.

Scope (whats in/out)
In scope:
- New incremental response frames (assert, update, commit) and a handshake extension for thermostat preferences.
- SDK surface: thermostat config, incremental stream consumer, commit/fallback events, simple adapters for typical frameworks (Node, Python).
- Telemetry slices and alerting for partial-commit regressions.
Out of scope:
- Full-fledged client-side orchestration UI (we will provide hooks only).
- Deep model-level orchestration changes (initial rollout will use existing model variants).

API/Protocol primitives (proposal)
- request.headers: thermostat: {mode, target_latency_ms, fidelity_target}
  - mode: [latency|balanced|fidelity|adaptive] (adaptive: server auto-tunes)
  - target_latency_ms: integer hint for first-frame latency budget
  - fidelity_target: short string e.g. summary-lite | summary-full | extractive | structured-form
- Response frames (streaming or chunked):
  - ASSERT frame: light structured payload that is safe to render and contains schema metadata + provisional confidence scores. Intended for immediate UX display.
  - UPDATE frame(s): additional structured patches, each with a patch-id and optional provenance (tool: name). UPDATE can be speculative.
  - COMMIT frame: canonical final payload, merges previous updates. Marks the session as closed for that request.
  - SOFT-ABORT frame: indicates a deliberate early stop (used when fidelity budget exceeded or timeouts).
- Frame metadata: each frame includes a small vector of {confidence_score, cost_delta_estimate, tool_tags}. Keep metadata compact (max ~200 bytes per frame).

Tool-calling model
- Tools are invoked server-side after initial ASSERT when thermostat indicates higher fidelity and budget allows. Tools are labeled with a cost bracket (cheap|moderate|expensive) and a determinism flag.
- Server will prefer cheap tools for UPDATE frames and reserve expensive / deterministic tools for COMMIT unless the mode==fidelity or SDK explicitly enables eager-tooling.
- If a tool is non-deterministic, server marks updates as non-committal unless re-run deterministically in COMMIT stage.

SDK ergonomics (the thermostat)
- SDK thermostat knobs:
  1) target_latency_ms (int) — soft target for first display
  2) fidelity_bias (float -1..1) — negative favors low-latency partials; positive favors full fidelity
  3) allowed_tool_classes (list of strings) — optionally restrict which tool cost brackets the server may use
- Default SDK behaviors:
  - Node/Python SDKs expose a StreamingResponse object with three callbacks: on_assert(frame), on_update(frame), on_commit(frame). There is also on_fallback(reason).
  - High-level helper: response.withPrefetch({thermostat}) that returns a small state machine to manage UI reconciliation.
- UX advice for developers:
  - Render ASSERT immediately as a compact card (title + short body) and show a progress indicator for updates.
  - Treat UPDATE frames as patching content; only replace if COMMIT arrives or confidence score crosses a threshold.

Observability and quality checks
- New metrics: percent_requests_with_update, avg_time_to_commit, percent_committed_after_tool, cost_delta_per_request.
- Alerts: sudden drop in commit rate for a route; large divergence between ASSERT and COMMIT (semantic drift).
- Evals: run A/B on fidelity modes with golden prompts and structured schemas to detect regressions. Tie to Redwood Optimize rule engine for auto-suggest thermostat defaults.

Backward compatibility and fallbacks
- If client doesnt support thermostat headers, server falls back to balanced mode and returns a single COMMIT frame (legacy behaviour).
- If SDK sees SOFT-ABORT or no COMMIT within N ms (configurable), it fires on_fallback and can optionally request a re-run with fidelity_bias=1.

Operational considerations
- Capacity: tools invoked as part of UPDATEs should be accounted in billing separately per tool-class. Need cheap-tool pool reservation to meet target_latency_ms.
- Rate limiting: thermostat-aware rate limits (higher request rate allowed for latency mode but fewer expensive tool credits).
- Security: tool provenance must be auditable — frame metadata tracks tool id and execution trace id.

Migration plan (pilot)
1) Phase 0 (2 weeks): spec ship + internal SDK prototypes (Node, Python).
2) Phase 1 (4 weeks): small internal pilots with Solutions teams on 3 routes (search-snippet, email-compose, question-answer). Monitor metrics.
3) Phase 2 (6–8 weeks): open beta for select customers; tweak thermostat defaults via Redwood Optimize.
4) Phase 3: GA when commit-rate and perf SLOs met, plus SDKs have adapter templates for React/Next/React Native.

Open questions / tradeoffs
- How large can frame metadata be before it impacts streaming performance? (need infra bench).
- Should we standardize a small typed schema language for ASSERT frames (lightweight subset of JSON-schema) or rely on string schemas?
- Billing model for incremental tool calls: per-tool vs per-commit amortized. Product to decide.
- How do we reconcile non-deterministic tool updates for critical flows (legal/financial)? Option: disallow non-deterministic tools unless commit-only.

Acceptance criteria (initial)
- SDKs implement thermostat surface and streaming callbacks; internal teams can integrate with <= 2 dev-days.
- Pilot routes show first-byte assert latency within 15% of baseline and commit-rate >= 70% for balanced mode.
- Telemetry surfaced in Console with new dashboards and alerting rules for commit drift.

Appendix: small example (pseudo)
Request headers:
  thermostat: {mode: \"latency\", target_latency_ms: 120, fidelity_target: \"summary-lite\"}
Stream frames (example):
  ASSERT {\"title\":\"Key points\",\"body\":\"3 bullets\",\"schema\":\"summary-v1\",\"confidence\":0.72}
  UPDATE {\"patch_id\":\"u1\",\"changes\":[{\"op\":\"add\",\"path\":\"/body/1\",\"value\":\"extra detail\"}],\"tool\":\"wiki-extract\",\"confidence\":0.64}
  COMMIT {\"title\":\"Key points\",\"body\":\"3 bullets — enriched\",\"schema\":\"summary-v1\",\"confidence\":0.88}
Notes to reviewers
- This is intentionally sketchy. Please focus feedback on: SDK surface ergonomics, obvious security/operational gaps, and acceptance targets that feel unrealistic.
- Slack thread: #hosted-api-toolflow (see linked artifacts).
